The proposed carpet cloak uses alternating layers of silicon (εr = 17.1) and a Low Index Material (εr = 0.55).
The cloak operates at a visible wavelength of 534 nm.
Using LIM layers reduces the cloak height by a factor of 2.3 compared to a cloak without LIM layers.
The cloak conceals a triangular object with height-to-width ratio h2/a = 0.5.
Quantum dots used are CdSe/CdS core coated with silver shell nanoparticles.
Quantum dots act as gain media to compensate for silver loss in the LIM.
The polymer host medium for the nanoparticles is polyethylene glycol with εhost = 2.11.
Effective permittivity of the LIM is calculated using Clausius–Mossotti relation and Mie theory.
Numerical simulations confirm the LIM has real permittivity ≈ 0.55 and imaginary permittivity ≈ 0.003 at 534 nm.
The carpet cloak works effectively for incident angles from 0° to 60°.
Metasurface-based carpet cloaks typically operate only for incident angles up to 15°.
The background medium permittivity in the proposed cloak is air (εr = 1), unlike some previous designs requiring εr = 1.8.
The cloak is designed for TM-polarized light with the magnetic field perpendicular to the x–y plane.
Full-wave numerical simulations use Gaussian beam illumination and PEC boundary conditions for the ground plane.
The cloak mimics reflection from a flat surface, making the cloaked object invisible to an observer.
The height ratio of the cloak to the object in previous conventional designs is more than 5, while it is about 2 in this design.
The cloak's anisotropic dielectric properties are realized by multilayer alternating isotropic dielectrics following effective medium theory.
The scattering coefficient A1 of the core–shell nanoparticles is calculated using Mie theory with Ricatti-Bessel functions.
The cloak's performance is numerically validated using Comsol Multiphysics and CST software.
Losses in the cloak are mainly due to silicon layers but can be mitigated by material choice at the cost of cloak thickness.
